# Mitigating the impact of conference and travel cancellations on researchers’ futures ## Authors - Tracey Weissgerber1 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-7490-2600](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7490-2600)) † - Yaw Bediako3 ([ORCID: 0000-0001-9786-7564](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9786-7564)) - Charlotte M de Winde4 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-8318-4612](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-8318-4612)) - Hedyeh Ebrahimi5 ([ORCID: 0000-0003-3647-7356](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3647-7356)) - Florencia Fernández-Chiappe6 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-1577-0804](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1577-0804)) - Vinodh Ilangovan7 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-3445-5383](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3445-5383)) - Devang Mehta8 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-8911-1174](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-8911-1174)) - Carolina Paz Quezada9 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-0260-5754](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0260-5754)) - Julia L Riley10 ([ORCID: 0000-0001-7691-6910](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7691-6910)) - Shyam M Saladi12 ([ORCID: 0000-0001-9701-3059](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9701-3059)) - Sarvenaz Sarabipour13 ([ORCID: 0000-0001-5097-5509](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5097-5509)) - Andy Tay14 ([ORCID: 0000-0003-3652-9515](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3652-9515)) ### Affiliations 1. Department of Biomedical Engineering, National University of Singapore Singapore Singapore † Corresponding author ## Abstract The need to protect public health during the current COVID-19 pandemic has necessitated conference cancellations on an unprecedented scale. As the scientific community adapts to new working conditions, it is important to recognize that some of our actions may disproportionately affect early-career researchers and scientists from countries with limited research funding. We encourage all conference organizers, funders and institutions who are able to do so to consider how they can mitigate the unintended consequences of conference and travel cancellations and we provide seven recommendations for how this could be achieved. The proposed solutions may also offer long-term benefits for those who normally cannot attend conferences, and thus lead to a more equitable future for generations of researchers. ## Prioritize refunds We recognize that conference cancellations may have a severe impact on organizations’ and societies’ finances, though we ask that they endeavor to issue refunds of registration fees promptly. If needed, refunds should be prioritized for those researchers who are most likely to be experiencing financial hardship in this difficult time. Researchers from countries with limited funding, graduate students and postdoctoral researchers tend to be the lowest paid and are perhaps more likely to have covered the costs of attending these meetings out of their own pocket (Malloy, 2020). These groups’ risk of financial hardship may be exacerbated by the fact that those with limited resources are often obligated to book the cheapest flights and accommodation, which may not be eligible for refunding or rebooking. For meetings that are not canceled, refunds of registration fees should be given to those who are unable to attend due to travel bans, or who choose not to attend for reasons of personal safety and public health. We ask that any society or organization that is currently facing financial difficulties still give registrants the option to request a refund or, where applicable, choose to have their fee ‘roll forward’ for next year’s event (Hines, 2020). We would advise those in this situation to be transparent about the expected impact on their finances; some registrants may choose to donate the money to keep the organization afloat. ## Reimburse all costs associated with canceled travel Funders should allow researchers to obtain reimbursement for canceled travel, even if the cancellation is voluntary. Agencies such as the Canadian Tri-Council have recently adopted such measures and may serve as an example (Fraser and Sauvé-McCuan, 2020). Funders who have already awarded travel grants to ECRs or scientists from countries with limited research funding could allow the recipients to defer the use of these funds for an additional year. In addition, visa fees can be prohibitively expensive, disproportionately impact researchers from countries with limited research funding, and often are not covered by funding agencies and travel grants. We therefore urge funders that do not currently cover visa fees to consider revising these policies, and to do so retroactively to assist researchers facing financial hardship due to conference and travel cancellations. ## Cover remaining expenses Institutions can help by reimbursing ECRs for expenses that will not be covered by conference organizers or funding agencies. ECRs who paid in advance may find that registration fees will not be refunded, that their funding agency or travel grant will not allow reimbursement, or that their travel arrangements cannot be canceled. Institutions may also consider offering advances to ECRs who are awaiting refunds or reimbursement from conference organizers, travel providers and funding agencies. Obtaining refunds may be a lengthy process, as many organizations lack clear policies and staff to handle large-scale cancellations. Providing advances on refunds and reimbursements will reduce stress and financial hardships for ECRs with limited resources. ## Go virtual While established researchers are more likely to have symposium talks that can be carried forward to the next year, early-career researchers often present research projects that may be published before the next conference. Canceling or postponing meetings may cost ECRs their one opportunity to present their research. For this reason, we ask that conference organizers consider making canceled in-person conferences virtual instead. For example, talks could be given via videoconferencing and poster sessions could be hosted online (Table 1). **Table 1.** Ideas for virtual conferences.
Option Example(s)
Organize virtual poster sessions with live video and chat options. Cognitive Neuroscience Society (2020)
Make abstracts, posters, and other conference materials freely available online for anyone to read and share. SOT 2020 (Hines, 2020)
Allow speakers to offer a pre-recorded talk for any online session. Provide instructions for recording a talk. Invite pre-recorded speakers for a live Q and A session after their virtual talk, at a time that accommodates the speaker’s time zone. Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI Foundation/IAS–USA, 2020)
Organize a virtual conference, followed by a virtual ‘unconference’ where scientists interact with others in small groups that are automatically matched based on similar interests. Neuromatch 2020
Organize a free virtual conference using social media and videoconferencing. Librarians Building Momentum for Reproducibility (2020) with draft guidance following their organizing experience available from Sayre et al. (2020) 1st International Twitter Conference of Herpetology (Associação Portuguesa de Herpetologia, 2018)
_This is not an exhaustive list._ We are aware that switching meetings to a virtual setting would likely place an additional burden on the conference organizers, who are already dealing with the logistical and financial impact of cancellation. One solution to this problem may be to invite ECRs and researchers from countries with limited research funding to join committees to organize the online events. This may provide those individuals with valuable career development and networking experience. ## Livestream for remote participation Conferences that are not canceled should be livestreamed. This would allow scientists, who cannot – or no longer wish to – travel, to participate virtually. Ideally, organizers should allow new registrations from people who did not register initially because they were unable to attend in person. ## Move networking online Conferences also provide important opportunities to network, attend workshops and interview for positions. Delaying these opportunities until next year may have long-term consequences for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, who only have a few years to complete their projects and plan the next phase of their career. Conference organizers should therefore look into hosting virtual networking events that would allow small groups of ECRs and researchers from countries with limited research funding to interact with more senior researchers. ## Give recognition Being selected to present at a conference is one of the ways that the scientific community recognizes the work of an individual researcher. The scientific community should agree that researchers can list conference activities on their CVs, even if the conference was canceled or the researcher was unable to attend. This is particularly important for conference activities that will not be published, though conference organizers should make abstract books freely available online, and speakers could consider sharing their slides or recordings of their talk with the community. While we hope that these suggestions may alleviate some of the anxiety and disruption caused by COVID-19, we also encourage the scientific community to consider a global perspective. Our current reliance on in-person conferences for networking and career development creates systemic inequalities between those who have the resources to attend conferences regularly and those who do not. Many scientists in developed countries are now pausing to consider the opportunities that they will miss out on as they cancel their travel plans. As we reflect on this, it is important to remember that these experiences are routine for scientists in countries with limited research funding, as well as for those with disabilities or chronic illnesses that limit their attendance at scientific meetings. We hope that the widespread disruptions resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic will draw attention to the challenges that our more vulnerable colleagues regularly encounter. For instance, several of the measures suggested above are necessary because ECRs are routinely required to pay for conferences and travel out of their own pocket before seeking reimbursement several months later. This is an insurmountable financial barrier for many ECRs and scientists from countries with limited research funding (Malloy, 2020). We hope that this crisis leads to widespread adoption of new policies to pay ECRs for conferences and travel costs upfront. We also hope that the research community will learn from this experience by developing and refining alternatives to in-person conferences (Table 1). While the current emphasis is on online formats, we must also recognize that 46% of the global population has no internet connectivity (ITU, 2020). We thus need solutions that do not depend on reliable internet access as this may create further barriers for researchers who do not have high speed internet (Bohannon, 2016). This includes some scientists in countries with limited research funding, and those working in remote or rural areas. The number of scientists with difficulties accessing the internet may also increase as more people begin working from home. In addition to helping those who cannot attend conferences due to COVID-19, new solutions could also offer long-term benefits for researchers who normally cannot attend conferences. This includes researchers who are disabled, have chronic diseases, care for family members, or researchers who experience problems caused by visa restrictions or a lack of funding. While slowing the spread of this new virus and caring for those who require medical care must remain our top priority, the current challenges we face as a scientific community may also offer new opportunities to build a more equitable global community for the scientists of tomorrow.

results.result: Conference and travel cancellations disproportionately affect early-career researchers (ECRs) and scientists from countries with limited research funding due to their lower pay, greater likelihood of self-funding conference attendance, and limited ability to book refundable travel options. Additionally, visa fees are prohibitively expensive for researchers from countries with limited funding and are often not covered by funding agencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C6 are supported by citation to Malloy (2020), while C2, C3, C7, C10, and C11 represent reasonable inferences about the differential financial impacts on vulnerable researcher populations. The logical chain connecting lower pay, self-funding practices, non-refundable bookings, and visa fee burdens provides coherent support for the disproportionate impact claim.

results.result: Conference cancellations have greater career consequences for ECRs compared to established researchers because ECRs often present research that may be published before the next conference, losing their opportunity to present, and delays in networking opportunities have long-term career impacts given the limited timeframe of graduate and postdoctoral training.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C14 and C21-C22 form a coherent argument about differential career impacts. C22 is supported by general knowledge of training timelines, while C12-C14 and C21 represent reasonable inferences about the asymmetric consequences of cancellations. The logic connecting presentation timing, publication cycles, and career development windows is sound.

results.result: The current reliance on in-person conferences creates systemic inequalities, as scientists from countries with limited funding and those with disabilities or chronic illnesses routinely miss opportunities due to inability to attend conferences.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 present a coherent argument about structural inequalities in the conference system. While these are inferences rather than empirically demonstrated findings, they represent well-reasoned conclusions about accessibility barriers. The claims are internally consistent and align with documented disparities in conference access.

results.result: ECRs are routinely required to pay conference and travel costs out of pocket before reimbursement months later, which constitutes an insurmountable financial barrier for many ECRs and scientists from countries with limited research funding.
results.evaluation: Claim C27 is stated as factual knowledge about reimbursement practices, and C28 is supported by citation to Malloy (2020). Together they establish both the practice and its consequences for vulnerable researchers.

results.result: Virtual conference solutions face limitations because 46% of the global population lacks internet connectivity, and internet-dependent solutions may create barriers for researchers in countries with limited funding or remote/rural areas. The number of scientists with internet access difficulties may increase with remote work.
results.evaluation: Claim C29 is supported by data from ITU (2020), and C30 is supported by citation to Bohannon (2016). Claims C31-C32 represent reasonable knowledge-based assertions about internet access disparities. C33 is speculative but plausible. The overall argument about limitations of virtual solutions is well-supported.

results.result: The Canadian Tri-Council has adopted measures allowing researchers to obtain reimbursement for canceled travel, even if cancellation is voluntary.
results.evaluation: This claim is directly supported by citation to Fraser and Sauvé-McCuan (2020), providing a concrete example of policy adaptation.

results.result: Conference cancellations may severely impact organizations' finances, and obtaining refunds may be lengthy due to lack of clear policies and staff. Providing advances on refunds and reimbursements would reduce stress and financial hardship for ECRs with limited resources.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C41, and C42 represent reasonable inferences about organizational challenges and potential solutions. While not empirically demonstrated, these are logical conclusions about the financial and administrative consequences of mass cancellations and the benefits of advance payments.

results.result: Being selected to present at a conference is one way the scientific community recognizes individual researcher contributions.
results.evaluation: This claim represents established knowledge about academic recognition practices and is uncontroversial within the scientific community.

results.result: New solutions to in-person conferences could offer long-term benefits for researchers who are disabled, have chronic diseases, care for family members, or face visa restrictions or funding limitations, potentially leading to a more equitable future for researchers.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C40 are explicitly speculative about potential future benefits of alternative conference formats. While the reasoning is plausible, these represent hoped-for outcomes rather than demonstrated results. No evidence is provided that such solutions will actually be implemented or achieve the proposed equity benefits.

results.result: The COVID-19 pandemic has necessitated conference cancellations on an unprecedented scale.
results.evaluation: This claim represents factual knowledge about the scale of conference cancellations during the COVID-19 pandemic, which is well-documented and uncontroversial.

results.result: Visa fees can be prohibitively expensive.
results.evaluation: This claim represents general knowledge about visa costs and is stated as a factual assertion that is widely recognized in discussions of international research mobility.

results.result: While slowing the spread of COVID-19 and caring for those requiring medical care must remain the top priority, current challenges may offer opportunities to build a more equitable global scientific community.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 is a value statement about priorities, while C44 is speculative about potential positive outcomes. The speculation is reasonable but represents hoped-for rather than demonstrated outcomes.
